history.heading: Kingdoms of Nubia
paragraphs: Sudan's Nile Valley was home to the ancient civilisation of Nubia. The Kingdom of Kush ruled Egypt as its 25th dynasty in the 8th century BCE, and from Meroë it built more pyramids than Egypt; the sites of Meroë and Gebel Barkal are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Christian Nubian kingdoms flourished from the 6th century until the spread of Islam. The Funj Sultanate of Sennar ruled from the 16th century.

history.heading: Ottoman-Egyptian rule and the Mahdi
paragraphs: Egypt under Muhammad Ali conquered Sudan in 1821. In 1881 Muhammad Ahmad declared himself the Mahdi and led an uprising that captured Khartoum in 1885, killing British general Charles Gordon. The Mahdist state ruled until British-led forces defeated it at Omdurman in 1898. Sudan then became an Anglo-Egyptian condominium.

history.heading: Independence and conflict
paragraphs: Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956. It has experienced repeated coups and long civil wars between the north and the south, which led to South Sudan's independence in 2011. Omar al-Bashir ruled from 1989 to 2019, imposing Islamist rule; the conflict in Darfur from 2003 involved mass atrocities, and he was indicted by the International Criminal Court for genocide.

Mass protests overthrew Bashir in 2019, but the military seized power in a 2021 coup. In April 2023 war broke out between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The war has killed tens of thousands, displaced over 10 million people and caused famine, one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. The RSF took El Fasher in Darfur in October 2025 amid reports of mass killings.

culture.heading: Arab and African heritage
paragraphs: Sudan blends Arab and African identities. Arabic and English are official languages, and many other languages are spoken. Most people are Sunni Muslims, with Sufi orders important; whirling dervish ceremonies in Omdurman are famous. Novelist Tayeb Salih's Season of Migration to the North is a classic.
Ful medames (fava beans) and kisra (flatbread) are staples. Hospitality and coffee (jebena) ceremonies are important.

politics.heading: Civil war
paragraphs: Sudan has been torn by war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the RSF, led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti). Both sides are accused of serious abuses; the US determined that the RSF committed genocide in Darfur. The RSF set up a rival government in 2025, and foreign powers back different sides.

economy.heading: War economy
paragraphs: Before the war, Sudan's economy relied on agriculture (sorghum, sesame, gum arabic, of which it is the world's top producer, and livestock) and gold. The war has devastated industry, agriculture and infrastructure, including in Khartoum. Gold trade fuels the conflict. Inflation is very high, and most of the population needs humanitarian aid. The currency is the Sudanese pound.
